questions.question: What were the benefits and limitations of English being the medium of instruction in Indian colleges? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Benefits - Serves as a unifying link across India’s linguistic diversity, performing a role similar to
  • what Sanskrit did in ancient times - Allows students and scholars to read and compare literatures
  • from different regions (e.g., a Malayalam speaker reading Bengali works) through a common
  • language - Enables the "discovery" of regional texts by translating them into a medium that can
  • reach a national and global audience. Limitations - Created a "split sensibility" where students
  • knew more about Western classics than their own local literary traditions - Mukherjee argued that
  • using a secondary language can stifle "creative spontaneity," leading to imitation of Western models
  • rather than original Indian thought - Created a "great divide" between the English-speaking elite and
  • the majority of the population who speak bhashas (mother tongues). [U] / [CO1]

questions.question: How does the story "Open It!" illustrate the psychological devastation of war? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• The short story "Khol Do" ("Open It") by Saadat Hasan Manto - a powerful and
  • disturbing portrayal of the psychological devastation caused by war and the horrors of
  • Partition in 1947 - uses the tragic fate of a young girl, Sakina, and the despair of her father,
  • Sirajuddin, to reveal how deeply war can scar the human mind and soul.
  • Loss of identity and humanity – Sakina, a victim of rape and severe trauma - loses touch
  • with normal emotional or social responses. When the doctor says "Khol do" (open it),
  • intending it as an instruction for the window, Sakina responds by instinctively loosening
  • her shalwar cord — showing how she has been conditioned by repeated abuse – this
  • moment captures the brutal destruction of her sense of self and autonomy.
  • Mental breakdown of the father - Sirajuddin's psychological torment central to the story -
  • loses his wife in the chaos of Partition - obsessively searches for his daughter - his hope,
  • desperation, and final joy upon seeing her move are tragically misplaced — he interprets
  • her movement as life returning, unaware of what she has endured - inability to grasp the
  • extent of her trauma shows the psychological denial and helplessness war inflicts on
  • survivors.
  • Dehumanization of victims - soldiers who rescue Sakina are initially seen as saviours -
  • later implied they are her abusers - war corrupts – protectors turned into predators - moral
  • decay - reveals how war dehumanizes individuals, blurring the lines between right and
  • wrong, protector and violator.
  • Symbolism of life and speech - Sakina is silent, a symbol of countless voiceless victims.
  • When she finally responds to “Khol do,” it’s not a return to consciousness, but a
  • conditioned, tragic reflex. Her silence speaks volumes about psychological trauma —
  • sometimes so deep that it silences the soul. (CO3)

questions.question: Analyze the role of silence and unspoken trauma in conveying the story's message "Open It!" / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• In “Open It!” by Saadat Hasan Manto, silence shows the deep trauma the characters have gone
  • through. Sakina’s lack of response at the end reveals that her suffering is so severe that she cannot
  • express it in words. This silence makes the message clear: the violence of events like the Partition
  • of India leaves lasting emotional wounds that remain unspoken but deeply felt. [U] / [CO3]

questions.question: Describe Muthu Pattar’s internal reaction to seeing Murugesan’s success and how it reflects cultural expectations about age and pride. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• In “The Man Who Could Not Sleep” by Perumal Murugan, Muthu Pattar feels a deep, quiet
  • disturbance when he sees Murugesan’s success. Outwardly, he remains composed, but internally he
  • experiences hurt and a sense of diminished importance, as a younger man has surpassed him. His
  • pride is affected because he believes that age should naturally command respect and higher status.
  • This reaction reflects cultural expectations where elders are seen as more accomplished and
  • deserving of recognition. Murugesan’s rise unsettles this belief, creating an inner conflict in Muthu
  • Pattar between accepting change and holding on to traditional ideas of age, pride, and dignity.
  • [U] / [CO4]

questions.question: How did English education in British India shape Indian literature and culture? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Indian literature influenced by English and Western writings - Translated works
  • from different regional languages to English made people experience and study various
  • literatures - English emerged as link language and benefitted writers especially educated
  • people - Our culture acquired and adopted adaptions from England and the Western
  • world. (CO1)

questions.question: What role does English play in the development of India's link literature, according to Mukherjee? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• English provides a shared linguistic space where literatures from different Indian languages
  • (Bhashas) can meet and be compared - It acts as the primary "target language" for translations,
  • allowing a Tamil work to be read by a Kashmiri speaker, thereby creating a pan-Indian literary
  • consciousness - It "liberates" regional masterpieces from their linguistic borders, elevating "local"
  • classics to the status of "national" classics - It enables Comparative Literature within India, helping
  • scholars identify common themes, myths, and movements (like the Bhakti movement) that exist
  • across different Indian languages. .
  • [U] / [CO1]

questions.question: What message does Bhasa convey about the nature of victory and defeat? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Bhasa in “The Shattered Thigh” questions the assumptions about dharma and adharma -
  • dramatizes the mace duel between Bhima and Duryodhana at the end of the
  • Kurukshethra war. Krishna’s interference changed the course of the Kurukshethra war.
  • When Bhima was about to lose, Krishna signals him about Duryodhana’ s thigh. Bhima
  • strikes Duryodhana’s thigh and defeats him which is against the rules of ‘dharma’ - this
  • incident significant in stripping away the glory of Kurukshethra war as a war based on
  • dharma - play questions the futility of pride and the devastating impact of war.
  • Duryodhana presented with a tinge of tragic heroism - his characterization deviates from
  • the conventional image of the antagonist of The Mahabharata - victory and defeat are
  • relative and purely context bound - conflict arises between sense of duty and
  • righteousness - Bhima wins against Duryodhana but cannot escape the indictment of
  • violating the rules of war - the very idea of ‘victory’ in war sounds meaningless.
  • (CO2)

questions.question: Does Bhasa present Duryodhana as a villain seeking redemption, or as a noble warrior accepting his fate? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Bhasa moves away from the traditional "evil" portrayal, framing Duryodhana as a tragic hero rather
  • than a spiteful antagonist - He does not complain about Bhima’s "foul play" (hitting below the belt).
  • He accepts his broken thighs as the inevitable result of fate and the war - His interaction with his
  • son, Durjaya, shows a tender, fatherly side. He tells his son to abandon the old hatreds, prioritizing
  • the child's peace over his own ego. - When Ashwatthama wants to continue the slaughter of the
  • Pandavas, Duryodhana stops him, signaling that his thirst for blood has ended. He views his death
  • not as a punishment, but as a warrior’s transition. He dies with a vision of heaven, signifying he has
  • achieved the status of a noble hero.
  • [U] / [CO2]

questions.question: Discuss the themes of morality and humanity in Manto’s work, particularly in "Khol Do," and how they challenge societal norms. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Manto’s Urdu short-story “Khol Do!” (translated in English as “Open It!”) recounts a
  • poignant event related to the traumatic experience of Partition - depicts the unbearable
  • anguish, savagery and trauma of Partition - a powerful narrative which deals with the
  • division of the country and its aftermath - provides a unique perspective about the
  • atrocities committed - Manto presents violence as violence - cannot be termed as “Hindu
  • violence against Muslims” or vice versa - articulates his opinion that it was human
  • violence against human beings. People who suffered because of the Partition were first
  • human beings, not communal or religious beings - killings targeted against some “other”
  • community or race or religion - cannot be approved - animalistic nature of human beings
  • who not only sadistically enjoy others’ suffering but also partake and aggravate it.
  • (CO3)

questions.question: Describe two specific ways the text conveys the psychological impact of violence on characters, citing examples from the story "Open It!". / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• In “Open It!” by Saadat Hasan Manto, the psychological impact of violence is conveyed in two
  • clear ways. First, through Sakina’s numb and automatic response at the end—when she reacts to the
  • words “open it” without awareness—it shows how deeply trauma has affected her mind, reducing
  • her ability to think or feel normally. Second, through Sirajuddin’s confused and fragile mental state,
  • as he clings to hope and fails to fully grasp what has happened, the story shows how violence can
  • distort reality and leave a person emotionally shattered. [U] / [CO3]

questions.solution_html:
• Poem ‘Fungus’, the protagonist lies inside the cold and dark room - lives
  • isolated from the bright and warm outdoors - protagonist compares himself to a fungus -
  • reflects a deep existential loneliness and alienation - fungus can be interpreted as a
  • metaphor for psychological decay or moral corruption. (CO4)

questions.question: How does the author use memory, setting, and sensory detail to illustrate the contrast between Muthu Pattar’s past contentment and his present unease? / [CO4] [15x2 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• In “The Man Who Could Not Sleep” by Perumal Murugan, the author contrasts Muthu Pattar’s past
  • and present through memory, setting, and sensory detail. Through memory, Pattar recalls a time
  • when his life felt stable and satisfying, when he was respected and secure in his place. These
  • recollections highlight how content and confident he once was and how peacefully he slept in those
  • days. The setting shifts to his present surroundings, which feel restless and unsettling, especially at
  • night, reflecting his disturbed state of mind and inability to sleep. Finally, sensory details—such as
  • the silence of the night, small sounds, and his physical discomfort—intensify his unease, making his
  • anxiety feel immediate and real. Together, these elements clearly show the contrast between his
  • earlier peace and his current inner turmoil. [U] / [CO4]
  • [15x2 = 30]
